query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase high-entropy alloy (HEA) that is compositionally complex, prolonged high‐temperature cyclic loading induces strain‐assisted short‐range redistribution of solute atoms at grain boundaries, promoting incipient clustering and local ordering. This microstructural change reduces boundary cohesion and triggers brittle behavior – a mechanism distinctly different from the static grain-boundary segregation or intermetallic precipitation seen in conventional alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single‐phase high-entropy alloy with a uniformly distributed multi-principal element mixture and no detectable grain-boundary phases.
generation.intervention: Subject specimens to controlled cyclic mechanical loading at elevated temperatures while maintaining the overall composition.
generation.conditions: Service-like conditions that involve elevated temperature and cyclic (or dynamic) loading over time, in contrast to isothermal aging without mechanical deformation.
generation.structural_mediator: Strain-induced short-range ordering or nanocluster formation at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: High temperature combined with cyclic loading accelerates atomic mobility in the otherwise sluggish diffusion HEA. The applied strain promotes localized rearrangement of elements at grain boundaries, creating regions of short-range order or early-stage clustering that reduce interatomic cohesion. This localized embrittlement compromises toughness even though the bulk alloy remains single-phase and avoids coarse intermetallic formation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to an unloaded (or minimally loaded) baseline sample, the cyclically loaded HEA will exhibit a measurable decrease in fracture toughness and ductility. Microstructural analysis (e.g., via transmission electron microscopy or atom probe tomography) will reveal signs of localized compositional modulation or nanoscale clustering at grain boundaries.
generation.baseline: The same HEA aged isothermally at the same temperature but without cyclic loading, expected to maintain a homogeneous microstructure with high toughness.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is predicted to operate under high-temperature service conditions with significant cyclic or dynamic mechanical loading. At lower temperatures or under static conditions, the driving force for strain-induced short-range ordering may be insufficient to trigger observable embrittlement.
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical loading amplitude, temperature threshold, and time scale required for the onset of significant grain-boundary ordering are not precisely known. There is also uncertainty regarding the relative contribution of mechanical versus thermal activation to the clustering process.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical single-phase HEA specimens. Subject one set to prolonged cyclic mechanical loading at an elevated temperature that simulates service conditions, while aging the second set under the same thermal conditions without cyclic loading. Conduct fracture toughness tests on both sets and perform high-resolution microstructural analyses (using TEM and atom probe tomography) focused on grain boundaries.
measurements: Fracture toughness and ductility (e.g., crack tip opening displacement)
Microstructural characterization of grain-boundary regions (detection of clustering or short-range order)
Comparison of compositional homogeneity at grain boundaries between loaded and unloaded specimens
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cyclically loaded specimens do not show a statistically significant reduction in fracture toughness or detectable evidence of grain-boundary clustering compared to the unloaded specimens, then the hypothesis that strain-induced short-range ordering leads to embrittlement in this HEA is falsified.
